summary_html: Court issues a **protective or restraining order** to prevent contact, remove abuser, or ensure safety without removing the child. Federal law leaves implementation to states but funds protection efforts through CAPTA and IV-B.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — authorizes protective interventions and state plan requirements  
- **SSA Title IV-B** — permits funding for protective services and court interventions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the Court set out the ex parte petition, preliminary hearing and probable-cause hearing sequence under § 40-11-7.1 and held that the twelve-month period for termination may run from the child's placement in DCYF care rather than from a formal finding of abuse or neglect.
key_cases.relevance: The Family Court is authorized to make interim orders in its discretion respecting the rights of the child pending the probable-cause hearing.
key_cases.quote: Next, a hearing on the petition must be held within seven days.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: A parent's familial-integrity right includes the right to prompt post-deprivation process after an emergency separation; the state actor who prolonged the separation without any hearing was not entitled to qualified immunity at summary judgment, while the prosecutor was.
key_cases.relevance: Interim orders restricting contact must themselves be reviewable promptly; an unreviewed no-contact posture is the defect Suboh condemns.
key_cases.quote: Even when there are such exigent circumstances, there must be an adequate post-deprivation hearing within a reasonable time.

key_cases.holding: The Court vacated the portion of the termination decree resting on the mother's mental deficiency under § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) for lack of legally competent evidence, affirmed unfitness on another ground, and quashed as moot DCYF's certiorari petition about ending visitation pending appeal.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses the Family Court's suspension of a parent's visitation privileges on DCYF's motion, the mechanism by which contact is restricted short of removal.
key_cases.quote: Reversing the Family Court's decision to terminate Mary Ann's parental rights pursuant to § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) (mental deficiency), we vacate that portion of the TPR decree.
